title: The forest monks
hookLine: the Thai forest tradition: monks in the jungle, keeping the old rules closely
last: TIPITAKA — A BOOK MADE OF MARBLE.

cards: So much of the Buddha's life happened under trees. He was born, the story goes, in a grove, his mother holding a branch. He woke up under a tree.
He gave his first teaching in a deer park. He died lying between two trees in a forest. The early monks lived in forests, slept at the roots of trees, and walked into villages only to collect food.
Over the centuries many monasteries moved into towns and cities, and that's natural. But about a hundred years ago, in the northeast of Thailand, a handful of monks walked back into the jungle.

teach.h: AJAHN MUN WALKS INTO THE FOREST.
teach.b: The best-known was Ajahn Mun, born in 1870 in Isan, the region of Thailand near the Lao border. Ajahn means teacher.

With his own teacher, Ajahn Sao, he chose a hard life: wandering on foot through the forests of Thailand and Laos, sleeping under a cloth tent hung with a mosquito net, meditating through the night, and keeping the monastic rules as closely as the old texts describe.
The forests then were full of tigers, snakes and malaria.
The practice has an old name, dhutanga, a set of voluntary austerities listed in the commentaries: eating one meal a day, eating only from the bowl, living at the foot of a tree.
Monks who took up the wandering life were called thudong monks, from that word. Ajahn Mun trained a generation of students.
One of them, Ajahn Chah, founded a forest monastery in 1954 near the city of Ubon, and later a monastery for foreign monks.
Through his students, forest monasteries now stand in England, Australia, New Zealand, the United States and beyond, where monks still walk for alms in the morning.

teach.h: AJAHN CHAH AND THE STILL POOL.
teach.b: Ajahn Chah liked to compare a trained mind to a still forest pool, where all kinds of wild animals come to drink, and you can watch them clearly. Most of the forests Ajahn Mun walked through have since been cut down.
The monasteries became islands of trees.
And the tradition keeps a simple conviction: the Buddha's teaching began in the forest, and the forest remembers.

how: In Thai forest monasteries in Thailand and abroad, monks eat one meal a day from the alms bowl, practice walking and sitting meditation, and keep the monastic rules strictly; lay visitors often come to stay and practice.

games.q: match each name to the forest tradition.
p: walked the forests of Thailand and Laos

s: the Buddha's life has almost nothing to do with forests
born in a grove, awake under a tree, died between two trees.
forest monasteries now stand in England and Australia
forest monks eat one meal a day from the bowl

games.q: you're a young monk in Thailand a hundred years ago. your comfortable town temple is pleasant, but you want to practice as the early monks did. what does Ajahn Mun do?
o: stay in town and read about forests.
walk into the forest, keeping the old rules closely.
games.why: Ajahn Mun wandered the forests of Thailand and Laos, facing tigers and malaria, and trained a generation of forest monks.

practice: Picture a forest monastery: a clearing among tall trees, a simple wooden hall open on the sides, a swept path where a monk walks slowly back and forth, cicadas, a distant bird, cool early air.
Then let the picture fade and imagine your mind as a still forest pool. Thoughts come to drink like animals at the edge; you don't chase them, you watch.

wordCard.voice: Arañña. The forest: where the Thai forest monks, following Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah, kept the old rules closely, deep among the trees.

orig.note: Pali arañña: forest, wilderness; a forest monk is an araññavāsī, a forest dweller.

carryVoice: Your line: the forest remembers. Watch the pool; don't chase what comes to drink. Day two hundred ninety-three.
